title.en: Do not call a heuristic route optimal

summary: Say which method produced a route and what that method guarantees, especially when the scene shows a best path.
objective: Keep routing scenes honest about the difference between a computed optimum, a bounded heuristic and a hand-authored path.
applies_when: A pick tour, delivery route, patrol path or cable run is presented as good or best.
A route is recomputed when the user changes the targets.
A comparison between two routes is displayed.
example_prompts: Show an efficient pick tour and say how it was computed.
Compare my route against a better one.
negative_signals: Scenes where the path is decorative and no efficiency claim is made.
Shortest-path problems on a graph with a stated exact algorithm, where the guarantee is real.
not_for: Scenes where the path is decorative and no efficiency claim is made.
Shortest-path problems on a graph with a stated exact algorithm, where the guarantee is real.

principles: Optimal is a mathematical claim about a stated objective under stated constraints. Without both, the word means nothing a viewer can check.
Three very different things look identical on screen: an exact solution for a small instance, a heuristic tour, and a path someone drew. The scene should distinguish them.
A route is optimal only with respect to its own cost function. A shortest-distance tour may be a poor route once aisle direction, congestion or handling time are included.
Comparison is more useful than a label: showing the improvement over a baseline tells the viewer more than an unverifiable claim of optimality.
implementation: Name the method and the objective on the artifact: exact search on this many stops, nearest neighbour with two-opt improvement, or an authored demonstration path.
Display the cost in its units and, where a baseline exists, the improvement against it.
For small instances where exhaustive search is cheap, offer it explicitly so the viewer can see the gap between the heuristic and the true optimum.
State the constraints actually modelled, such as one-way aisles, capacity or time windows, and mark any that are ignored.
Recompute the route when the inputs change instead of leaving a stale path with a stale label.
observable_checks: Ask the scene for its objective function; a route that cannot state what it minimises is not making a checkable claim.
On a small instance, compare the shown route with an exhaustive search result; a heuristic labelled optimal will eventually differ.
Add one stop and confirm the route and the reported cost both update.
Change a constraint that is supposedly modelled, such as blocking an aisle, and confirm the route responds.

creative_affordances: Heuristics are the right engineering answer at realistic sizes; the rule only asks that the label match the method.
Showing the search process itself, including rejected candidates, is often more instructive than the final route.
known_limits: Authored honesty guidance about claims; it asserts no complexity result and provides no algorithm.
It does not evaluate whether a particular heuristic is appropriate for a given instance size.
